consensus_summary: Faith primarily means trusting reliance and confident assurance in God/Christ (especially for justification/salvation), not mere intellectual assent; alternatives include faithfulness/loyalty, the body of doctrine, living faith issuing in works, and faith as gift.
book_summary: Faith is trusting faithfulness: reliance on God’s unseen promise that is held steady and brought to life through obedience.
consensus_core_identification: trusting reliance/assurance in God and Christ as the instrument of justification
book_core_identification: trusting faithfulness (reliance on the unseen promise constitutively steadied and vivified by obedience)
boundary_disagreement: Book treats obedience as intrinsic to what keeps and enlivens faith itself, whereas consensus typically keeps bare trust as the core referent and locates works as necessary fruit, evidence, or perfection of living faith rather than part of the definitional core.
rationale: Both identify the same basic referent (reliance on God’s unseen promise/Christ). The book preserves that category but materially tightens its extension and conditions by fusing faithfulness/obedience into the definition (“trusting faithfulness… held steady and brought to life through obedience”), thereby excluding or reclassifying bare trust or “dead” faith that the broader consensus still counts as faith (even while criticizing it). This is boundary refinement, not replacement of the central idea or a wholly new referent.
strongest_objection: Consensus (and the book’s own common-view note) treats justification-by-faith passages as establishing trust alone as the core instrument, with James/Hebrews obedience texts describing the necessary outworking rather than redefining faith itself as ‘trusting faithfulness.’
